modules.title: Getting Started with Word
modules.content:
## From a Blank Page to a Finished File

Imagine you have a brilliant idea for a community newsletter, a formal letter to a landlord, or a detailed grocery list for a holiday feast. You have the thoughts ready, but you need a place to put them. For decades, Microsoft Word has been the industry standard for this task. 

At its simplest, Word is a **word processor**. Unlike a basic text editor (like Notepad), a word processor allows you to not only type text but to control exactly how that text looks, how it is organized on a page, and how it is shared with others. Whether you are writing a one-sentence note or a hundred-page manuscript, the process always begins with the same fundamental steps: navigating the interface, starting a document, and ensuring your work is saved securely.

## Navigating the Word Interface

When you first open Microsoft Word, the screen can feel overwhelming. There are buttons, tabs, and bars everywhere. However, the interface is designed logically, dividing tools into specific zones based on how often you need them.

### The Ribbon: Your Command Center
The most prominent feature at the top of the window is the **Ribbon**. The Ribbon is a wide band of tools and icons organized into **Tabs**. 

Think of the Ribbon as a digital toolbox. Instead of having every single tool visible at once—which would clutter the screen—Word groups related tools together. For example:
*   **File Tab:** This is the only tab that takes you away from your document to a "backstage" view where you manage files (saving, opening, and printing).
*   **Home Tab:** This is the default tab. It contains the most frequently used tools, such as font styles and alignment.
*   **Insert Tab:** Use this when you want to add something *into* the page, such as a picture or a table.

Each Tab contains **Groups**. For instance, on the Home Tab, you will see a group called "Font" that clusters all the tools for changing text size and color. A single button within a group is called a **Command**.

### The Quick Access Toolbar: Your Shortcuts
Located above or below the Ribbon (depending on your version), the **Quick Access Toolbar (QAT)** is a small, customizable row of buttons. 

The QAT is designed for "one-click" efficiency. By default, it usually contains the **Save** icon (a small floppy disk) and the **Undo** arrow (which reverses your last action). If you find yourself using a specific command repeatedly, you can right-click that command in the Ribbon and select "Add to Quick Access Toolbar" to keep it permanently visible, regardless of which tab you are currently using.

### The Status Bar: The Document’s Vital Signs
At the very bottom of the Word window is a thin strip called the **Status Bar**. While it may seem insignificant, it provides real-time information about your document:
*   **Page Count:** Tells you which page you are currently on and how many pages exist in total (e.g., "Page 1 of 3").
*   **Word Count:** Displays the total number of words in the document. Clicking this will open a detailed statistics box.
*   **View Shortcuts:** On the right side of the status bar, you can switch how the document looks on your screen (such as "Read Mode" for easier reading or "Print Layout" to see exactly how it will look on paper).
*   **Zoom Slider:** A sliding bar that allows you to zoom in to see text more clearly or zoom out to see multiple pages at once.

## Creating Your First Document

Once you launch Word, you are greeted with the **Start Screen**. You aren't immediately placed on a blank page; instead, you are given a choice of how to begin.

### Starting with a Blank Document
For most projects, you will choose **Blank Document**. This opens a clean, white digital sheet of paper. This is the best choice when you want total control over the layout or when you are writing something simple, like a letter or a rough draft.

### Using Templates
A **Template** is a pre-designed document that already has formatting, layouts, and sometimes "placeholder text" (text that tells you where to type your own information). 

Templates are incredibly useful for professional documents where a specific structure is expected. Examples include:
*   **Resumes:** Pre-set margins and headings that make your experience look polished.
*   **Brochures:** Pre-divided columns and image placeholders.
*   **Calendars:** Perfectly aligned grids for the current month.

To use a template, browse the gallery on the Start Screen or search for a specific keyword (e.g., "Invoice") in the search bar. Once selected, you simply click on the existing text and replace it with your own.

## Managing Your Files

Creating a document is only half the battle; you must know how to store it so you can find it later and share it with others.

### Saving Your Work
Saving is the process of writing your digital work onto your computer's hard drive or a cloud service (like OneDrive).

**Save vs. Save As**
Beginners often confuse these two commands, but they serve very different purposes:
1.  **Save:** Use this when you have already named your file and just want to update it with the newest changes. It overwrites the previous version of the file.
2.  **Save As:** Use this the *first time* you save a document, or when you want to create a *copy* of a document while keeping the original unchanged. **Save As** allows you to choose the file name, the folder where it is stored, and the file format.

### Understanding File Formats
When you use "Save As," you can choose the **File Format** (the type of file). The two most common formats in Word are:

**1. .docx (Word Document)**
This is the standard, editable Word format. Use this for any document that you plan to keep working on. It preserves all your formatting, images, and edits.

**2. .pdf (Portable Document Format)**
A PDF is a "digital print." Once a file is saved as a PDF, it cannot be easily edited by others. Most importantly, a PDF looks exactly the same on every device—whether it is opened on a Mac, a PC, or a smartphone. 
*   **Scenario:** If you are sending a resume to a potential employer, save it as a **PDF**. This ensures the employer sees your perfect formatting exactly as you intended, and they cannot accidentally delete a line of your text.

### Opening and Closing Files
To return to a project you started previously:
1.  Click the **File** tab.
2.  Select **Open**.
3.  Navigate to the folder where you saved the file and double-click the file name.

When you are finished, you can close the document by clicking the **X** in the top right corner of the window. Word will prompt you to save your changes if you haven't done so recently—always click "Save" if you have made updates you want to keep.

## Practical Scenario: The Community Flyer

To put these concepts together, let's look at a realistic workflow:

**The Goal:** Create a flyer for a neighborhood garage sale.

1.  **Launch:** You open Word and see the Start Screen.
2.  **Choose:** Instead of a blank page, you search the **Templates** for "Flyer." You select a colorful design that looks inviting.
3.  **Navigate:** You use the **Ribbon** (Home Tab) to change the date and time of the sale. You glance at the **Status Bar** to make sure the flyer is only one page long.
4.  **Save (Initial):** You go to **File > Save As**, name the file "Garage_Sale_Flyer," and save it as a **.docx** file in your "Documents" folder. This allows you to come back and change the date later if needed.
5.  **Save (Final):** You want to email the flyer to your neighbors. To ensure the layout doesn't shift when they open it, you go to **File > Save As** and select **PDF** from the format dropdown menu.
6.  **Close:** You click the **X** to close Word, knowing your work is safely stored in two different formats.

## Key Takeaways

*   **The Ribbon** is the main menu at the top, organized into Tabs and Groups.
*   **The Quick Access Toolbar** provides one-click shortcuts for common tasks like Save and Undo.
*   **The Status Bar** at the bottom tracks page count, word count, and zoom levels.
*   **Blank Documents** are for starting from scratch; **Templates** provide pre-made professional layouts.
*   **Save** updates an existing file; **Save As** lets you name a new file or change its format.
*   **.docx** files are for editing; **.pdf** files are for sharing and final presentation.

modules.title: Basic Text Entry and Editing
modules.content:
## Putting Words on the Page

Imagine you have just opened a **Blank Document**. You have a great idea for a letter, a report, or a story, but the page is a vast, blinking white void. The blinking vertical line you see is called the **Insertion Point**. 

The insertion point is the most important visual cue in a **word processor**. It tells you exactly where the next character you type will appear. If you don't see it, you aren't ready to type. As you press keys on your keyboard, the insertion point moves to the right, "pushing" the text forward.

### Typing Your First Sentences
To begin, simply start typing. Word handles the "flow" of text automatically. You do not need to tell the computer when to move to the next line; when you reach the right edge of the page, Word performs a **Word Wrap**. This means it automatically moves the entire word to the next line so you don't have to.

**Essential Keyboard Keys for Text Entry:**
*   **Spacebar:** Adds a single blank space between words.
*   **Enter Key:** This does not just create a space; it creates a **Paragraph Break**. Use this when you want to start a new paragraph or move down to a new section.
*   **Shift Key:** Hold this down while pressing a letter to make it uppercase, or press it while hitting a punctuation key (like the number 1 key to get an exclamation point).
*   **Caps Lock:** Press this once to type everything in uppercase. Press it again to return to lowercase.

### Correcting Mistakes: Deleting and Overwriting
Errors are a natural part of writing. In Word, you have two primary ways to remove text, depending on where your insertion point is located.

**1. The Backspace Key**
The **Backspace** key deletes characters to the **left** of the insertion point. Think of it as "erasing backward." If you type "Happpy" and realize there is an extra 'p', place your insertion point after the third 'p' and hit Backspace.

**2. The Delete Key**
The **Delete** key removes characters to the **right** of the insertion point. This is useful when you have moved your cursor to the beginning of a word or sentence and want to clear everything ahead of it.

**Overwriting Text**
To "overwrite" or change a word, you must first select the text you want to replace (see the "Selecting Text" section below). Once the text is highlighted, any key you press—including a letter or a space—will instantly replace the selected text with the new input.

---

## Selecting Text

Before you can move, copy, or change text, you must first tell Word which specific part of the document you are talking about. This process is called **Selecting**. When text is selected, it usually appears with a colored background (often blue or gray), while the rest of the document remains white.

### Using the Mouse for Selection
The mouse is the most intuitive tool for selecting text, especially for beginners.

*   **Single Word:** Double-click the left mouse button on the word.
*   **Single Line:** Move your mouse to the left margin (the white space to the left of your text). Your cursor will change from an "I-beam" to a right-pointing arrow. Click once.
*   **A Paragraph:** Triple-click anywhere inside the paragraph.
*   **Large Blocks of Text:** Click at the beginning of the section you want to select, hold down the left mouse button, and drag the mouse to the end of the section.

### Using the Keyboard for Selection
Keyboard selection is often faster once you become comfortable with it. To select using the keyboard, you must hold down the **Shift** key while moving the insertion point.

*   **Character by Character:** Hold **Shift** and press the **Left** or **Right Arrow** keys.
*   **Word by Word:** Hold **Shift** + **Ctrl** and press the **Left** or **Right Arrow** keys.
*   **Line by Line:** Hold **Shift** and press the **Up** or **Down Arrow** keys.

---

## Moving and Duplicating Text

Often, you will realize that a sentence belongs in a different paragraph, or you want to use the same phrase multiple times without re-typing it. This is where **Cut**, **Copy**, and **Paste** come in.

### The Clipboard Concept
When you Cut or Copy text, Word doesn't just move it; it places a temporary copy of that text in a hidden storage area called the **Clipboard**. The text stays on the Clipboard until you replace it with something else or close the program.

### Cut vs. Copy
While they seem similar, they perform very different actions:

*   **Cut:** This removes the selected text from its original location and places it on the Clipboard. Use this when you want to *move* text.
*   **Copy:** This leaves the original text exactly where it is and places a duplicate on the Clipboard. Use this when you want to *duplicate* text.

**How to perform these actions:**
1.  **Select** the text you want to move or duplicate.
2.  Go to the **Home Tab** and look at the **Clipboard Group**.
3.  Click the **Cut** command (scissors icon) or the **Copy** command (two-page icon).

### Pasting Text
Once text is on the Clipboard, you can place it anywhere in your document.

1.  Move your **Insertion Point** to the exact spot where you want the text to appear.
2.  Go to the **Home Tab** and click the **Paste** command (the clipboard icon).

**Scenario: Rearranging a Letter**
Imagine you wrote a formal letter, but you realized the "Thank you for your time" sentence is at the top of the page instead of the bottom. 
*   **Step 1:** Select the sentence "Thank you for your time."
*   **Step 2:** Click **Cut** in the Home Tab. The sentence disappears from the top.
*   **Step 3:** Scroll to the bottom of the letter and click after the final sentence.
*   **Step 4:** Click **Paste**. The sentence now appears at the end of the letter.

---

## Undoing and Redoing Mistakes

One of the most powerful features for a beginner is the ability to "travel back in time." If you accidentally delete a whole page or paste text in the wrong place, you do not have to manually fix it.

### The Undo Command
The **Undo** command reverses your last action. If you just deleted a paragraph by mistake, clicking Undo will bring it back instantly.

*   **Via the Ribbon:** Go to the **Home Tab** and click the curved arrow pointing left.
*   **Via the QAT:** Click the **Undo** button on the **Quick Access Toolbar**.
*   **Keyboard Shortcut:** Press **Ctrl + Z**.

### The Redo Command
Sometimes, you might Undo an action and then realize that the "mistake" was actually correct. The **Redo** command reverses the Undo. It essentially "re-does" the action you just erased.

*   **Via the Ribbon:** Go to the **Home Tab** and click the curved arrow pointing right.
*   **Keyboard Shortcut:** Press **Ctrl + Y**.

*Note: Redo only works if you have used Undo immediately before it. If you Undo a mistake and then type something new, you can no longer Redo the previous action.*

---

## Key Takeaways

*   The **Insertion Point** (blinking line) indicates where text will appear.
*   **Backspace** deletes to the left; **Delete** deletes to the right.
*   **Word Wrap** automatically moves text to the next line, while the **Enter** key creates a new paragraph.
*   **Selecting** text is required before you can Cut, Copy, or Overwrite.
*   **Cut** moves text; **Copy** duplicates it; **Paste** places it from the Clipboard.
*   **Undo (Ctrl+Z)** is the fastest way to fix a mistake; **Redo (Ctrl+Y)** restores an action that was undone.

modules.title: Formatting Characters and Paragraphs
modules.content:
## Making Your Document Stand Out

Imagine you have written a professional letter to a potential employer. You have the right words and the correct spelling, but every single letter is the same size, the same plain black color, and every line starts exactly at the left margin. To a reader, this looks like a "wall of text"—it is intimidating, lacks hierarchy, and doesn't guide the eye to the most important information.

**Formatting** is the process of changing the visual appearance of your document to make it more readable, professional, and organized. While the *content* is what you say, the *formatting* is how you present it. By changing the look of individual characters and the arrangement of paragraphs, you can turn a plain slab of text into a polished document.

## Formatting Characters

Character formatting refers to changes made to individual letters, words, or phrases. To change the appearance of a specific piece of text, you must first tell Word which text you want to change. This is done through **Selecting**.

To select text, click and hold your left mouse button at the start of the word or sentence, drag the cursor to the end of the desired area, and then release the button. The selected text will appear highlighted in gray.

### Changing Font Style and Size

The **Font** is the design of the characters in your document. Different fonts convey different moods: some look formal and traditional, while others look modern or casual.

1. Ensure you are on the **Home Tab**.
2. Look for the **Font Group**.
3. Click the drop-down arrow next to the **Font Name box** (which usually says "Calibri" or "Arial" by default).
4. Scroll through the list and click on a font that suits your needs.
    * *Tip: For professional documents, stick to clear, easy-to-read fonts like Times New Roman, Arial, or Calibri.*

Right next to the font name is the **Font Size box**. This determines how large or small your characters appear.
* To change the size, click the drop-down arrow and select a number. A larger number means larger text.
* Alternatively, you can use the **Increase Font Size** (a large 'A') or **Decrease Font Size** (a small 'A') buttons to nudge the size up or down one step at a time.

### Adding Emphasis with Bold, Italic, and Underline

Sometimes you need certain words to "pop" so the reader notices them immediately. This is called **Emphasis**. In the **Font Group**, you will find three primary tools for this:

* **Bold (B):** This makes the text thicker and darker. Use this for headings or key terms you want to define.
* **Italic (*I*):** This slants the text to the right. It is commonly used for book titles, foreign words, or to add a subtle emphasis to a word in a sentence.
* **Underline (U):** This places a horizontal line beneath the text. This is often used for hyperlinks or to draw heavy attention to a specific line.

You can combine these. For example, a main title might be both **Bold and Underlined**.

### Changing Text Color

Color can be used to categorize information or draw attention to a warning or a highlight. 

1. Select the text you wish to color.
2. In the **Font Group**, locate the **Font Color** command (represented by the letter 'A' with a colored bar underneath it).
3. Click the drop-down arrow to see the **Theme Colors** palette.
4. Click the color you want to apply.

*Warning: Be cautious with colors. Light yellow or neon green text on a white background is very difficult to read and can make a document look unprofessional.*

## Formatting Paragraphs

While character formatting focuses on the "small" details, paragraph formatting focuses on the "big" layout. Paragraph formatting affects the entire block of text, from the first word to the point where you pressed the Enter key.

### Text Alignment

**Alignment** refers to how the edges of your paragraph line up between the left and right margins of the page. You can find these options in the **Paragraph Group** on the **Home Tab**.

* **Align Left:** This is the default setting. Text starts at the left margin and leaves a "ragged" (uneven) edge on the right. This is the standard for most letters and reports.
* **Center:** Text is centered between the left and right margins. This is most commonly used for titles, cover pages, or invitations.
* **Align Right:** Text starts at the right margin and leaves a ragged edge on the left. This is often used for dates or addresses at the top of a formal letter.
* **Justify:** This stretches the text so that both the left and right edges are straight and flush against the margins. Word does this by adding tiny amounts of extra space between words. This is common in newspapers, textbooks, and formal legal documents.

### Line Spacing

**Line Spacing** is the amount of vertical space between the lines of text within a paragraph. If lines are too close together, the text feels cramped; if they are too far apart, the document feels disconnected.

To change the spacing:
1. Select the paragraph(s) you want to adjust.
2. In the **Paragraph Group**, click the **Line and Paragraph Spacing** command (an icon showing vertical arrows next to horizontal lines).
3. Select a number from the list:
    * **1.0 (Single Spacing):** The standard for most business documents.
    * **1.15 to 1.5:** Provides a bit more "breathing room" and is often easier to read on a screen.
    * **2.0 (Double Spacing):** Leaves a full blank line between every line of text. This is frequently required for academic essays so that teachers have room to write handwritten notes between the lines.

### Paragraph Indentation

An **Indentation** is the distance between the page margin and the edge of the text. The most common use of indentation is to signal the start of a new paragraph.

There are two primary ways to handle indentation:

**1. The Tab Key (First Line Indent)**
The simplest way to indent the first line of a paragraph is to click your cursor at the very beginning of the paragraph and press the **Tab key** on your keyboard. This pushes the first line to the right by a standard distance (usually half an inch).

**2. The Indent Commands**
If you want to move an *entire* paragraph further away from the margin, use the **Increase Indent** and **Decrease Indent** buttons in the **Paragraph Group**.
* **Increase Indent:** Pushes the whole paragraph to the right.
* **Decrease Indent:** Pulls the paragraph back toward the left margin.

## Putting it All Together: A Practical Scenario

Imagine you are creating a "Volunteer Flyer" for a local animal shelter. Here is how you would apply these formatting tools to make the flyer effective:

1. **The Title:** You type "VOLUNTEERS WANTED!" You select the text, change the **Font** to something bold and modern (like Arial), increase the **Font Size** to 24, **Center** the alignment, and change the **Font Color** to a bright blue.
2. **The Introduction:** You write a paragraph explaining the shelter's mission. You keep this **Left Aligned** for readability and use **1.15 Line Spacing** so it doesn't look crowded.
3. **Key Requirements:** You write a sentence saying, "Must be over 18 years old." To make sure no one misses this, you apply **Bold** to the phrase "over 18 years old."
4. **Contact Information:** At the bottom, you type the contact email and phone number. You use the **Align Right** command to tuck this information neatly into the bottom right corner of the page.

By combining these small changes, you have transformed a plain list of facts into a visual document that guides the reader's attention from the most important (the title) to the most specific (the contact info).

## Key Takeaways

* **Selection** is the essential first step; Word cannot format text unless you highlight it first.
* **Font** settings (Style, Size, and Color) change the appearance of individual characters.
* **Emphasis** tools (Bold, Italic, Underline) are used to highlight key information within a sentence.
* **Alignment** determines how text sits between the margins (Left, Center, Right, or Justified).
* **Line Spacing** controls the vertical gap between lines, affecting the overall density of the page.
* **Indentation** moves text away from the margin, often used to mark the start of a new paragraph or to shift an entire block of text.

modules.title: Working with Lists and Bullets
modules.content:
## Why Use Lists?

Imagine you are writing a grocery list or a set of instructions for assembling a bookshelf. If you wrote these as standard paragraphs, the reader would have to hunt through sentences to find the specific items or steps. It would look like this:

*First, you need to gather the screws and the wooden panels. Then, you should attach the side panels to the base. After that, slide the back panel into the grooves. Finally, tighten all the screws.*

Now, imagine the same information as a list:

1. Gather screws and wooden panels.
2. Attach side panels to the base.
3. Slide the back panel into the grooves.
4. Tighten all screws.

The second version is instantly easier to scan, understand, and follow. In Microsoft Word, lists allow you to break up dense blocks of text, highlight key points, and create a logical flow for your reader.

## Creating Bulleted Lists

A **bulleted list** (also known as an unordered list) is used when the order of the items doesn't matter. For example, a list of ingredients for a cake or a list of your favorite movies.

### Starting a New List
There are two primary ways to create a bulleted list in Word:

**Method 1: Starting from scratch**
1. Click on the document where you want the list to begin.
2. Go to the **Home Tab**.
3. In the **Paragraph Group**, click the **Bullets** command (the icon looks like three small dots next to three lines).
4. Type your first item.
5. Press the **Enter** key. Word will automatically create a new bullet point for you.

**Method 2: Converting existing text**
If you have already typed a list of items on separate lines:
1. Use your mouse to highlight (select) all the lines you want to turn into a list.
2. Go to the **Home Tab**.
3. Click the **Bullets** command in the **Paragraph Group**. Word will instantly add bullets to the start of every selected line.

### Ending the List
When you are finished with your list, you need to tell Word to stop adding bullets. You can do this in two ways:
* Press the **Enter** key twice at the end of your last item.
* Click the **Bullets** command again in the **Home Tab**.

## Customizing Bullet Symbols

You aren't limited to the standard solid black circle. Depending on the tone of your document—whether it's a formal business report or a casual invitation—you may want to change the symbol.

### Changing the Bullet Style
1. Click anywhere inside your existing list.
2. Go to the **Home Tab**.
3. Click the **small down arrow** next to the Bullets command. This opens the **Bullet Library**.
4. Select a new symbol (such as an open circle, a square, or a checkmark) from the library. Word will update every bullet in that list to the new symbol.

### Defining a New Bullet
If the library doesn't have the symbol you want, you can create your own:
1. Click the arrow next to the Bullets command.
2. Select **Define New Bullet...** at the bottom of the menu.
3. A dialog box will appear with three options:
    * **Symbol:** Allows you to choose from a vast library of characters (like arrows or stars).
    * **Picture:** Allows you to upload a small image from your computer to use as a bullet.
    * **Font:** Allows you to change the size or color of the bullet independently of the text.
4. Select your preferred option and click **OK**.

## Creating Numbered Lists

A **numbered list** (or ordered list) is used when the sequence of items is important. This is essential for step-by-step instructions, rankings, or agendas.

### Starting a Numbered List
The process for creating a numbered list is nearly identical to creating a bulleted list:
1. Go to the **Home Tab**.
2. In the **Paragraph Group**, click the **Numbering** command (the icon looks like "1 2 3" next to three lines).
3. Type your item and press **Enter**. Word will automatically provide the next number in the sequence.

### Changing the Numbering Format
Not every list needs to start with "1, 2, 3." You might prefer Roman numerals (I, II, III) or letters (a, b, c).
1. Click inside your numbered list.
2. Click the **small down arrow** next to the Numbering command.
3. Choose the format that best fits your needs from the library.

### Restarting or Continuing Numbering
Sometimes Word tries to be "too smart." If you start a new list further down in your document, Word might automatically start it at "4" because it thinks you are continuing a list from earlier.

* **To restart at 1:** Right-click on the number that is incorrect and select **Restart at 1**.
* **To continue a previous list:** Right-click on the number and select **Continue Numbering**.

## Nesting and Indentation

**Nesting** is the process of creating a "list within a list." This is often called a **multilevel list**. It is useful for outlines or complex instructions where a main step has several sub-steps.

### Creating Sub-levels (Increasing Indent)
To move a list item to a lower level (pushing it to the right):
1. Place your cursor at the beginning of the line you want to move.
2. Press the **Tab** key on your keyboard. 
3. Alternatively, go to the **Home Tab** and click the **Increase Indent** command in the **Paragraph Group**.

Word will automatically change the bullet symbol or the numbering format (e.g., changing "1" to "a") to show that this item is a sub-point of the one above it.

### Returning to a Higher Level (Decreasing Indent)
To move a sub-item back to the main list level (pulling it to the left):
1. Place your cursor at the beginning of the line.
2. Hold the **Shift** key and press **Tab**.
3. Alternatively, go to the **Home Tab** and click the **Decrease Indent** command in the **Paragraph Group**.

### Realistic Scenario: The Meeting Agenda
Imagine you are organizing a monthly team meeting. A simple list isn't enough; you need a hierarchy. Here is how you would build it using nesting:

1. **Welcome and Introductions** (Main Level)
    * *Introduction of new hires* (Press Tab to nest)
    * *Review of last month's goals* (Press Tab to nest)
2. **Project Updates** (Press Shift+Tab to return to Main Level)
    * *Website Redesign* (Press Tab to nest)
        * *Mobile responsiveness* (Press Tab again for a third level)
        * *Color palette update* (Press Tab again for a third level)
    * *Client Feedback* (Press Shift+Tab to return to second level)
3. **Closing Remarks** (Press Shift+Tab to return to Main Level)

## Adjusting List Alignment

Sometimes, the gap between the bullet and the text is too wide, or the list is too far from the left margin. While you can use the **Increase/Decrease Indent** buttons for general movement, you can fine-tune the position using the **Ruler**.

*(Note: If you do not see a ruler at the top of your document, go to the **View Tab** and check the box for **Ruler**.)*

On the Ruler, you will see two small markers (triangles) when you click inside a list:
* **First Line Indent (Top Triangle):** Controls where the bullet or number itself is placed.
* **Hanging Indent (Bottom Triangle):** Controls where the text begins.

By clicking and dragging these markers, you can precisely control the spacing of your list to ensure it aligns perfectly with the rest of your document's formatting.

## Key Takeaways

* **Bulleted Lists** are for items where the order does not matter.
* **Numbered Lists** are for sequences, steps, or rankings.
* Use the **down arrow** next to the list commands to change symbols or numbering formats.
* Use the **Tab** key to create a sub-level (nesting) and **Shift+Tab** to move back to a higher level.
* To stop a list, press **Enter** twice.
* Use the **Ruler** to make precise adjustments to the alignment and spacing of your list items.

modules.title: Page Layout and Setup
modules.content:
## Designing Your Page Canvas

Imagine you have spent an hour typing a beautiful, detailed report. You hit print, and as the paper slides out of the machine, you realize the text is crammed too close to the edges, making it look claustrophobic and unprofessional. Or, perhaps you’ve created a wide chart that looks great on your screen, but when printed, the right side of the chart is completely cut off because the page is too narrow.

Up until now, you have focused on the *content* of your document—the words, the fonts, and the lists. However, a document isn't just a collection of text; it is a physical object (or a digital file meant to mimic one). Before you finalize your work, you must define the "canvas" that your text sits on. This is called **Page Layout**.

Page Layout is the process of configuring the physical dimensions, the white space around your text, and the structural organization of your pages. All of these settings are found under the **Layout Tab** on the **Ribbon**.

## Understanding Margins

When you open a **Blank Document**, you will notice that your text doesn't start at the very top-left corner of the white page. There is a consistent border of empty space surrounding your typing area. This space is called the **Margin**.

**Margins** are the blank areas between the edge of the paper and the area where your text is placed. They serve two main purposes:
1. **Readability:** Text that runs from edge to edge is difficult for the human eye to track.
2. **Printing/Binding:** Most printers cannot print to the very edge of a page. Additionally, if you plan to put your document in a three-ring binder, you need extra space on the left side so the holes don't punch through your words.

### How to Adjust Margins

To change the margins of your document:
1. Click on the **Layout Tab**.
2. In the **Page Setup Group**, click the **Margins** command.
3. A drop-down menu will appear with several presets:
    * **Normal:** The standard setting (usually 1 inch on all sides).
    * **Narrow:** Reduces the margins to 0.5 inches, allowing you to fit more text on a single page.
    * **Moderate:** A middle-ground between Normal and Narrow.
    * **Wide:** Increases the margins, creating a narrower column of text (often used for formal letters or poetry).

If none of these presets work for your project, you can select **Custom Margins...** at the bottom of the menu. This opens a dialog box where you can type in the exact measurement (e.g., 1.25 inches) for the Top, Bottom, Left, and Right sides independently.

## Page Orientation: Portrait vs. Landscape

Depending on what you are creating, you may find that a standard vertical page isn't the best fit. Word offers two primary types of **Orientation**, which refers to the direction in which the document is displayed or printed.

### Portrait Orientation
**Portrait** is the default setting. The page is taller than it is wide. This is the standard for almost all business letters, essays, and reports.

### Landscape Orientation
**Landscape** flips the page sideways. The page is wider than it is tall. This is ideal for:
* Large tables or spreadsheets that have many columns.
* Certificates or diplomas.
* Foldable **Brochures**.

### Changing the Orientation
To switch the direction of your page:
1. Go to the **Layout Tab**.
2. In the **Page Setup Group**, click **Orientation**.
3. Select either **Portrait** or **Landscape**.

*Note: Changing the orientation affects the entire document. If you change one page to Landscape, every page in that document will become Landscape.*

## Selecting Paper Size

While most people use standard "Letter" size paper (8.5" x 11"), Word allows you to change the **Paper Size** to match whatever physical paper you are actually putting into your printer. 

If you set your document to "Legal" size in Word but put "Letter" size paper in your printer, the printer will likely cut off the bottom of your pages.

### How to Change Paper Size
1. Go to the **Layout Tab**.
2. In the **Page Setup Group**, click **Size**.
3. Choose from the list of common sizes:
    * **Letter:** The standard for North America.
    * **Legal:** Longer than letter (8.5" x 14"), often used for contracts.
    * **A4:** The international standard used in most countries outside North America.

If you are using specialty paper (like a small postcard or a large ledger), select **More Paper Sizes...** at the bottom of the menu to enter your own dimensions.

## Managing Page Breaks

As you type, Word automatically moves your cursor to the next page when you reach the bottom of the current one. This is called a "soft return." However, you cannot always predict exactly where the page will end.

Imagine you are writing a professional report. You have finished the "Introduction" section halfway down page 2, and you want the "Main Analysis" section to start exactly at the top of page 3. If you simply hit the **Enter** key repeatedly to push the text down, you create a mess. If you later go back and add a single sentence to the Introduction, all those "Enter" spaces will shift, and your "Main Analysis" header will now be awkwardly stuck in the middle of page 3.

To solve this, we use a **Page Break**.

A **Page Break** is a command that tells Word: "Stop this page right here and start the next piece of content on a brand new page," regardless of how much empty space is left.

### Inserting a Page Break
There are two ways to do this:
1. **Via the Ribbon:** Go to the **Insert Tab** (or the **Layout Tab**), and click **Page Break**.
2. **Via Keyboard Shortcut:** Press `Ctrl + Enter` on your keyboard. This is the fastest way to jump to a new page.

Once a Page Break is inserted, any text you add *above* the break will not push the start of the next page further down; the next page will always start at the very top.

## Organizing Content with Columns

Most documents are written in a single block of text that spans the width of the page. However, if you look at a newspaper, a magazine, or a professional brochure, you will see that the text is split into vertical sections. These are called **Columns**.

Columns are useful because shorter lines of text are often easier and faster for people to read. They are also essential for creating layouts that look more like a publication than a standard letter.

### How to Set Up Columns
1. Go to the **Layout Tab**.
2. In the **Page Setup Group**, click **Columns**.
3. Choose your preferred layout:
    * **One:** The standard full-width layout.
    * **Two:** Splits the page into two equal vertical halves.
    * **Three:** Splits the page into three equal vertical sections.
    * **Left/Right:** Makes one column narrower than the other (often used for sidebars in newsletters).

### Applying Columns to Specific Sections
By default, if you click "Two," Word will turn your entire document into two columns. However, you might want a title that spans the whole page, followed by two columns of text underneath.

To do this:
1. Highlight (select) only the specific text you want to split into columns.
2. Go to **Layout** $\rightarrow$ **Columns** and select your choice.
3. Word will automatically place "Section Breaks" around the highlighted text to ensure the rest of the document remains in a single column.

## Scenario: Creating a Community Newsletter

Let's put these tools together. Suppose you are volunteering to create a one-page newsletter for a local gardening club.

* **The Goal:** A professional-looking flyer that fits a lot of information but remains readable.
* **The Setup:**
    1. **Margins:** You choose **Narrow** margins because you have a lot of text and photos, and you want to maximize the available space.
    2. **Orientation:** You stick with **Portrait** because it will be handed out as a standard flyer.
    3. **Paper Size:** You ensure it is set to **Letter**, as that is what your home printer uses.
    4. **Columns:** You keep the "Club News" header as a single column across the top. Then, you highlight the "Upcoming Events" and "Gardening Tips" sections and set them to **Two Columns**. This creates a professional, magazine-style look.
    5. **Page Breaks:** You realize you've written a "Member Directory" at the end that is too long for the first page. You insert a **Page Break** to ensure the directory starts cleanly on page 2.

## Key Takeaways

* **Margins** are the white spaces around the edges of your page; they prevent text from being cut off during printing and improve readability.
* **Orientation** determines if your page is vertical (**Portrait**) or horizontal (**Landscape**).
* **Paper Size** must match the physical paper in your printer to avoid layout errors.
* **Page Breaks** (`Ctrl + Enter`) force the cursor to the start of the next page, ensuring your sections always start in the right place.
* **Columns** split your text into vertical blocks, which is ideal for newsletters, brochures, and magazines.

modules.title: Inserting Tables
modules.content:
## Organizing Information with Tables

Imagine you are tasked with creating a sign-up sheet for a neighborhood potluck. You need to collect the guest's name, the dish they are bringing, and whether they have any food allergies. If you simply typed this as a list, the page would quickly become a cluttered wall of text. However, if you organize this information into a grid—with clear columns for names and rows for each guest—the information becomes instantly readable and professional.

This is the primary purpose of a **Table**. In a word processor, a table is a grid of boxes used to organize text, numbers, or symbols so that the relationship between different pieces of data is clear at a glance.

### Understanding Table Anatomy

Before you create your first table, it is important to understand the three basic components that make up every table:

*   **Column:** A vertical block of cells. Columns run from the top of the table to the bottom.
*   **Row:** A horizontal block of cells. Rows run from the left side of the table to the right.
*   **Cell:** A single rectangular box where a row and a column intersect. This is where you actually type your content.

When you tell Word you want a "3x4 table," you are asking for 3 columns and 4 rows, which results in a total of 12 cells.

## How to Insert a Table

There are several ways to add a table to your document, depending on how much control you need over the size.

### Using the Grid Selector
The fastest way to create a small, simple table is by using the visual grid.

1. Place your cursor in the document exactly where you want the table to appear.
2. Click the **Insert Tab** on the **Ribbon**.
3. In the **Tables Group**, click the **Table** command.
4. A grid of squares will appear. Hover your mouse over the squares to highlight the number of rows and columns you need. For example, move your mouse three squares across and four squares down to create a 3x4 table.
5. Click the last square in your selection, and Word will instantly drop the table into your document.

### Using the Insert Table Dialog
If you need a table larger than the grid allows (which maxes out at 10 columns and 8 rows), use the manual entry method.

1. Go to the **Insert Tab** $\rightarrow$ **Table**.
2. Instead of hovering over the grid, click **Insert Table...** at the bottom of the menu.
3. A small dialog box will appear. In the **Number of columns** box, type the specific number you need.
4. In the **Number of rows** box, type the specific number you need.
5. Click **OK**.

## Editing Table Structure

Once a table is inserted, you will often realize you forgot a category or need an extra row for a new entry. You do not need to delete the table and start over; you can modify it on the fly.

### Adding Rows and Columns
There are two primary ways to add space to your table:

**Method 1: The Hover Button (Fastest)**
1. Move your mouse cursor just outside the border of the table, specifically between two existing rows or columns.
2. A small circle with a plus sign (**+**) will appear.
3. Click the **+** button to instantly insert a new row or column at that exact location.

**Method 2: The Layout Tab**
When your cursor is inside a table, two new tabs appear on the **Ribbon** under a section called **Table Tools**. These are the **Table Design Tab** and the **Layout Tab**. These tabs only appear when you are working inside a table.

1. Click inside a cell next to where you want the new space.
2. Go to the **Layout Tab**.
3. In the **Rows & Columns Group**, choose one of the following:
    *   **Insert Above:** Adds a row above your current cell.
    *   **Insert Below:** Adds a row beneath your current cell.
    *   **Insert Left:** Adds a column to the left.
    *   **Insert Right:** Adds a column to the right.

### Deleting Rows, Columns, and Tables
If you have excess space or made a mistake, you can remove elements easily.

1. Click inside the cell, row, or column you wish to remove.
2. Go to the **Layout Tab**.
3. Click the **Delete** command in the **Rows & Columns Group**.
4. Select the appropriate option from the dropdown menu:
    *   **Delete Columns:** Removes the entire vertical column.
    *   **Delete Rows:** Removes the entire horizontal row.
    *   **Delete Table:** Removes the entire grid and all content within it.

## Advanced Cell Manipulation

Sometimes, a standard grid isn't enough. You may want a single heading that spans across three columns, or you may need to divide one cell into two.

### Merging Cells
**Merging** is the process of combining two or more cells into one large cell. This is most commonly used for table titles.

1. Click and drag your mouse to highlight (select) the cells you want to combine.
2. Go to the **Layout Tab**.
3. In the **Merge Group**, click **Merge Cells**.
4. The borders between the selected cells will disappear, creating one large area.

### Splitting Cells
**Splitting** is the opposite of merging; it breaks one cell into multiple smaller cells.

1. Click inside the cell you wish to divide.
2. Go to the **Layout Tab**.
3. In the **Merge Group**, click **Split Cells**.
4. A dialog box will ask how many columns and rows you want to divide that specific cell into. Enter the numbers and click **OK**.

## Formatting and Styling Your Table

A default table is a simple black-and-white grid. To make your data easier to read, you can apply professional styles and customize the borders.

### Applying Table Styles
Word provides pre-made color schemes and formatting options called **Table Styles**.

1. Click anywhere inside your table to activate the **Table Tools** on the Ribbon.
2. Click the **Table Design Tab**.
3. In the **Table Styles Group**, click the **More** arrow (the small arrow at the bottom right of the style gallery) to see all available options.
4. Hover over different styles to see a live preview on your document. Click a style to apply it.

**Pro Tip: Table Style Options**
To the left of the styles gallery, you will see the **Table Style Options Group**. These checkboxes change how the style is applied:
*   **Header Row:** Adds a distinct, bold look to the top row to identify the data below.
*   **Total Row:** Adds a distinct look to the bottom row, useful for sums or final totals.
*   **Banded Rows:** Colors every other row (zebra-striping), which helps the eye track information across long rows.

### Customizing Borders and Shading
If the pre-made styles aren't exactly what you need, you can manually change the lines (**Borders**) and background colors (**Shading**).

**Changing Borders:**
1. Go to the **Table Design Tab**.
2. In the **Borders Group**, you can change the **Border Style** (solid, dashed, or double line), the **Line Weight** (thickness), and the **Pen Color**.
3. After choosing your style, click the **Borders** dropdown menu and select where you want the line applied (e.g., **Outside Borders** to put a thick box around the whole table, or **All Borders** to ensure every cell is outlined).

**Adding Shading:**
1. Select the specific cells or rows you want to highlight.
2. Go to the **Table Design Tab**.
3. Click the **Shading** command and select a color from the palette. This is an excellent way to highlight a "Total" row or a critical piece of information.

## Putting it All Together: A Practical Scenario

Let's apply everything we've learned. Imagine you are creating a **Weekly Study Schedule**.

1. **Insert:** You start by using the **Insert Tab** $\rightarrow$ **Table** grid to create a 6x5 table (6 columns for Monday–Friday and a "Time" column; 5 rows for different time slots).
2. **Modify:** You realize you forgot Saturday and Sunday. You go to the **Layout Tab** and click **Insert Right** twice.
3. **Merge:** You want a title at the top. You click **Insert Above** to add a new row, select all the cells in that top row, and click **Merge Cells**. You type "MY STUDY PLAN" and center the text.
4. **Style:** To make it look professional, you go to the **Table Design Tab**, select a "Grid Table 4 - Accent 1" style, and check the **Header Row** box.
5. **Refine:** You want the "Time" column to stand out, so you select that column and use the **Shading** tool to give it a light grey background.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Tables** are grids made of **Columns** (vertical), **Rows** (horizontal), and **Cells** (the intersection of the two).
*   Use the **Insert Tab** to create a table via the visual grid or the **Insert Table** dialog for larger grids.
*   The **Layout Tab** (under Table Tools) is used for structural changes, such as adding or deleting rows/columns and merging or splitting cells.
*   The **Table Design Tab** (under Table Tools) is used for visual changes, such as applying **Table Styles**, changing **Borders**, and adding **Shading**.
*   **Banded Rows** improve readability by alternating colors, while **Merging** allows for custom layouts like spanning headers.

modules.title: Adding Visual Elements
modules.content:
## Why Visuals Matter in Word

Imagine opening a report and seeing nothing but solid walls of text. Your eyes glaze over before reaching the third paragraph. Now imagine the same report, but with a strategically placed photo of a smiling team, a clean timeline diagram, or even a simple arrow pointing to a key statistic. Suddenly, the document isn’t just readable—it’s *engaging*. Visual elements transform flat text into something dynamic, memorable, and professional. Whether you're crafting a newsletter, a school project, or a business proposal, adding pictures, shapes, icons, and graphics helps your audience absorb information faster and retain it longer.

This chapter will guide you through the basics of inserting and enhancing visuals in Microsoft Word. By the end, you’ll be able to:
- Insert pictures and resize them to fit your document
- Use shapes and text boxes to highlight important points
- Insert icons and SmartArt to simplify complex ideas
- Crop images to focus on exactly what matters
- Move and arrange elements freely using text wrapping

Let’s begin with the most common visual you’ll likely use: **pictures**.

---

## Inserting and Resizing Pictures

Adding a picture to your Word document is easier than you might think. Whether it’s a photo from your phone, a logo from your company, or an image you found online, Word lets you bring it into your document in just a few clicks.

### Inserting a Picture from Your Computer

1. **Place your cursor** where you want the picture to appear.
2. Go to the **Insert Tab** on the Ribbon.
3. In the **Images group**, click **Pictures**.
4. Choose **This Device** (previously called "This Device" or "Picture from File" depending on your Word version).
5. A file explorer window will open. Navigate to the image you want, select it, and click **Insert**.

> 💡 *Tip: You can also drag and drop an image directly from File Explorer into your Word document. Just find the image, click and hold it, then drag it into the document and release.*

### Resizing a Picture

Once the image is in your document, you may need to make it larger or smaller to fit your layout.

1. Click once on the image to select it. You’ll see **handles**—small white squares—around the edges and corners.
2. To resize proportionally (so the image doesn’t stretch oddly), click and drag one of the **corner handles**.
3. To resize freely (which may distort the image), use the **side handles**.
4. Release the mouse when the image looks the way you want.

> 📝 *Note: Always use the corner handles when possible. This keeps the image’s proportions intact. If the image looks stretched or squished, you’ve likely used a side handle by mistake.*

### Adjusting Picture Position

After inserting, your picture may not sit exactly where you want. You might need to move it slightly or center it. To move the image:

- Click and drag the image to a new location.
- Use the **arrow keys** on your keyboard for fine-tuned movement (hold **Ctrl** to move in smaller increments).

> ⚠️ *Important: By default, Word treats images as if they’re sitting on the line of text—like a large character. That means if you type below it, the text will appear under the image. To move the image freely, you’ll need to change how it interacts with text using **text wrapping**.*

---

## Controlling Text Wrapping

Text wrapping determines how text flows around your image. Without proper wrapping, your layout can look messy or confusing.

### Common Wrapping Options

Click on your image to select it. You’ll see a small **Layout Options** icon (a square with text and an arrow) near the top-right corner of the image. Click it to see these choices:

- **In Line with Text**: The image behaves like a character in your paragraph. It can’t be moved freely, and text flows above and below it.
- **Square**: Text wraps around the image in a square shape, even if the image has transparent areas.
- **Tight**: Text wraps closely around the visible edges of the image.
- **Through**: Similar to Tight, but Word tries to wrap text into any gaps inside the image.
- **Top and Bottom**: Text appears only above and below the image, not beside it.
- **Behind Text**: The image appears behind your text, like a watermark.
- **In Front of Text**: The image appears on top of your text, covering it.

> 🔧 *Try this:*
> 1. Insert a picture.
> 2. Click the **Layout Options** icon.
> 3. Select **Square** or **Tight**.
> 4. Try dragging the image around. Notice how the text reflows around it.

### Using the Wrap Text Menu

You can also access wrapping options from the **Picture Format Tab** that appears when you select an image:

- Go to **Picture Format > Wrap Text**.
- Choose from the same list of options.

> ✅ *Best practice: Use **Tight** or **Square** when you want text to flow naturally around an image. Use **Behind Text** for subtle backgrounds or **In Front of Text** for decorative overlays (sparingly).*

---

## Working with Shapes and Text Boxes

Shapes and text boxes are powerful tools for drawing attention, organizing content, or adding visual structure to your document.

### Inserting a Shape

1. Go to the **Insert Tab**.
2. In the **Illustrations group**, click **Shapes**.
3. A dropdown menu appears with categories: **Lines**, **Basic Shapes**, **Block Arrows**, **Stars and Banners**, etc.
4. Select a shape (e.g., a rectangle or circle).
5. Click and drag in your document to draw the shape.

> 📏 *Tip: Hold **Shift** while dragging to create a perfect square or circle.*

### Resizing and Moving a Shape

- Click the shape to select it.
- Use the **corner handles** to resize proportionally.
- Click and drag the shape to reposition it.

### Adding Text Inside a Shape

- Right-click the shape and choose **Add Text**.
- Type your text directly inside the shape.
- Format the text using the **Home Tab** (e.g., change font, size, color).

### Using Text Boxes for Flexible Text Placement

Text boxes are like mini-documents within your document. They allow you to place text anywhere and move it freely.

1. Go to **Insert > Text Box**.
2. Choose a preformatted style or select **Draw Text Box**.
3. Click and drag to create the box.
4. Type your text inside.

> 💡 *Use text boxes for callouts, side notes, or text that needs to stand out from the main flow.*

---

## Enhancing Documents with Icons

Icons are small, simple graphics that represent actions, objects, or ideas—like a magnifying glass for “Search” or a floppy disk for “Save.” Word includes a built-in library of icons you can insert directly.

### Inserting Icons

1. Place your cursor where you want the icon.
2. Go to **Insert > Icons**.
3. A window opens showing hundreds of icons organized by category (e.g., Communication, Education, Technology).
4. Browse or search for an icon (e.g., type “lightbulb”).
5. Select the icon and click **Insert**.

Once inserted, you can:
- Resize it using corner handles
- Change its color using the **Picture Format Tab**
- Wrap text around it like any other image

> 🎨 *Tip: Icons are vector-based, so they stay sharp even when you resize them large.*

---

## Creating SmartArt Graphics

SmartArt is perfect for turning lists, processes, or concepts into clear, attractive visuals—without needing design skills.

### Inserting SmartArt

1. Go to **Insert > SmartArt**.
2. A gallery appears with categories like **List**, **Process**, **Cycle**, **Hierarchy**, etc.
3. Choose a layout (e.g., “Basic Process” for a step-by-step flow).
4. Click **OK**.

Word inserts a placeholder graphic with sample text. To customize:

- Click in any shape and type your own text.
- Add or remove shapes using the **SmartArt Design Tab**:
  - Use **Add Shape** to insert new steps or points
  - Use **Layouts** to change the overall structure

### Formatting SmartArt

Use the **SmartArt Design Tab** to:
- Change colors with **Change Colors**
- Apply different styles with **SmartArt Styles**
- Rearrange elements with **Promote** or **Demote** (in hierarchical layouts)

> 🧩 *Example: Create a simple org chart to show team roles in a proposal.*

---

## Trimming Images with the Crop Tool

Sometimes your image includes extra space or background that you don’t want. The **Crop Tool** lets you trim it down to the essential part.

### Using the Crop Tool

1. Select the image.
2. Go to **Picture Format > Crop**.
3. Black crop handles appear around the image.
4. Click and drag any handle inward to remove unwanted areas.
5. Press **Enter** or click outside the image to apply the crop.

> 🔄 *Tip: You can always un-crop by selecting the image and clicking **Crop > Reset**.*

> ⚠️ *Note: Cropping doesn’t delete pixels—it just hides them. You can always adjust the crop later.*

---

## Putting It All Together: A Real-World Example

Let’s say you’re writing a flyer for a bake sale.

1. You insert a **photo of your best-selling cupcakes** using **Insert > Pictures > This Device**.
2. You resize it using the **corner handles** so it’s not too large.
3. You set the wrapping to **Tight** so text flows around the image.
4. You add a **star shape** with text “Fresh Daily!” using **Insert > Shapes**.
5. You insert an **icon of a calendar** next to the event date.
6. You create a **SmartArt timeline** showing baking times.
7. You crop a photo of ingredients to focus on the chocolate chips.

Now your flyer is eye-catching, organized, and easy to read.

---

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- **Distorted images**: Always use corner handles when resizing.
- **Text overlapping images**: Use proper text wrapping.
- **Overusing visuals**: Too many images or icons can clutter your document.
- **Ignoring file size**: Large images can slow down your document. Consider compressing them if needed.
- **Not saving originals**: If you crop or edit an image, save the original elsewhere in case you need to revert.

---

## Quick Troubleshooting Guide

| Problem | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| Image won’t move freely | Check wrapping—set to **Square**, **Tight**, or **Behind Text** |
| Image is too big | Click and drag a corner handle inward |
| Text is behind the image | Set wrapping to **In Front of Text** or adjust layering |
| Can’t find an icon | Use the search bar in the Icons window |
| SmartArt text is too small | Select the text and increase font size using the Home Tab |

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Pictures** bring life to your document. Insert them via **Insert > Pictures > This Device** and resize using corner handles to maintain proportions.
- Use **text wrapping** (accessed via the Layout Options icon or Picture Format tab) to control how text flows around images. **Tight** and **Square** are ideal for most layouts.
- **Shapes and text boxes** help organize content and draw attention. Add text directly inside shapes or use text boxes for flexible placement.
- **Icons** are small, scalable graphics you can insert via **Insert > Icons** to represent ideas quickly and clearly.
- **SmartArt** turns lists and processes into professional visuals with minimal effort. Customize it using the **SmartArt Design Tab**.
- The **Crop Tool** (found in **Picture Format > Crop**) trims images to focus on the important parts without deleting data.
- Always check your document layout after adding visuals—use wrapping and layering to ensure everything looks clean and readable.

Visuals don’t just decorate your document—they communicate. With these tools, you can turn plain text into a document that’s not only informative, but inviting.

modules.title: Headers, Footers, and Page Numbers
modules.content:
Imagine opening a professional report or a school essay and noticing a clean, consistent title at the top of every page. Or perhaps you’ve seen a page number in the bottom corner of a document, making it easy to reference specific sections. These aren’t just design choices—they’re part of what makes a document **readable, professional, and organized**. In Microsoft Word, these repeating elements are called **headers** (at the top of the page), **footers** (at the bottom), and **page numbers**. Together, they help guide the reader and give your document structure.

Headers and footers are like the quiet helpers of your document: they don’t shout for attention, but they’re always there, quietly doing their job. Whether you're writing a business proposal, a school assignment, or a simple letter, using headers and footers can make your document look polished and intentional. And page numbers? They’re essential for longer documents—no one wants to guess which page they’re on when they’re trying to find a specific section.

But here’s the thing: headers and footers aren’t just for looks. They serve practical purposes too. A header might include your document’s title, your name, or the date—so every page clearly belongs to the same project. A footer might hold the page number, or even your company’s contact information. And when you use **automatic page numbering**, you never have to worry about manually updating it if you add or remove pages.

By the end of this chapter, you’ll know how to add, edit, and customize these elements with confidence. You’ll even learn how to make the first page different from the rest—perfect for title pages or cover sheets where you don’t want page numbers or headers showing up right away.

Let’s begin by understanding what headers and footers actually are, and where you can find them in Word.

---

### What Are Headers and Footers?

A **header** is a block of text or graphics that appears at the **top** of every page in a document. A **footer** does the same thing, but at the **bottom** of the page.

These aren’t just random chunks of text—they’re meant to repeat on every page (or most pages) to provide useful information. For example:

- A book chapter might have the chapter title in the header.
- A business report might have the company name and the report title.
- A school essay might include your name and the assignment title.

Footers often contain page numbers, legal disclaimers, or contact details.

> 📝 **Jargon Alert**: A **block of text** just means a section of words grouped together—like a heading, a date, or a short phrase.

Headers and footers are part of **page layout**—the way content is arranged on the page. Earlier, in *Page Layout and Setup*, you learned how to set margins and page size. Now, you’re working with content that sits *within* those margins, but repeats across pages.

---

### Accessing Headers and Footers in Word

You can add headers and footers from the **Insert tab** on the **Ribbon**. The Ribbon is the horizontal menu bar at the top of Word, with tabs like *Home*, *Insert*, and *Design*.

Here’s how to open the header or footer area:

1. Open a Word document or create a new one.
2. Click the **Insert tab** on the Ribbon.
3. In the **Header & Footer group**, you’ll see two buttons:
   - **Header** (for the top of the page)
   - **Footer** (for the bottom of the page)
4. Click **Header** or **Footer**, then choose a built-in style from the menu.

When you do this, Word automatically opens the **header or footer area** for editing. You’ll notice the rest of the document becomes slightly dimmed—this is called **graysed out**—to show that you’re working *inside* the header or footer, not in the main text.

You can type directly into this area. For example, in a header, you might type: *"Annual Sales Report – Q1 2025"*.

To exit the header/footer area and return to your main document, press the **Esc key** (Escape) on your keyboard, or click anywhere outside the header/footer area.

> 🔍 **Tip**: You can also double-click the top or bottom margin of the page to open the header or footer for editing—no need to go to the Ribbon.

---

### Adding a Header

Let’s add a simple header step by step.

#### Step-by-Step: Insert a Header

1. Open your document.
2. Click the **Insert tab**.
3. In the **Header & Footer group**, click **Header**.
4. From the dropdown menu, choose a style. You’ll see pre-designed options like:
   - Blank
   - Austin
   - Facet
   - Ion
   - Integral
   - etc.

   Pick **Blank** if you just want a clean space to start typing.

5. Type your text directly into the header area. For example:
   - *"Project Phoenix – Final Report"*
6. Press **Esc** to return to your main document.

Now, if you scroll down, you’ll see your header appears at the top of every page—even if you add more pages later.

> ✅ **Why use a style?**
> Built-in styles are pre-formatted with fonts, spacing, and alignment. Using them ensures your header looks professional and consistent with Word’s design language.

---

### Adding a Footer

Footers work the same way as headers, but they appear at the bottom of the page.

#### Step-by-Step: Insert a Footer

1. With your document open, go to the **Insert tab**.
2. In the **Header & Footer group**, click **Footer**.
3. Choose a style from the menu (e.g., **Blank**).
4. Type your content in the footer area. Common footer content includes:
   - Page numbers
   - Date
   - Your name or company
   - A short legal note (e.g., “Confidential”)
5. Press **Esc** to finish.

Now your footer appears on every page.

> 💡 **Pro Tip**: You can mix and match. Use a header for the title and a footer for page numbers—this is very common in reports and books.

---

### Inserting Automatic Page Numbers

Page numbers are one of the most useful features in Word because they update automatically. If you add or delete a page, the numbers adjust themselves—no manual typing required.

#### Step-by-Step: Add Page Numbers

1. Go to the **Insert tab**.
2. In the **Header & Footer group**, click **Page Number**.
3. From the menu, choose where you want the number to appear:
   - Top of Page (Header)
   - Bottom of Page (Footer)
   - Page Margins (left or right side)
   - Current Position (floating in the text)
4. Select a style. For example:
   - *Plain Number* – just the number
   - *Page X of Y* – shows “Page 1 of 5” etc.
5. The page number appears in the selected location.

You’ll notice that the header or footer area opens automatically when you insert a page number—this is normal.

> ⚠️ **Important**: If you don’t want a header or footer text, just delete it and leave the page number. You can have a footer with *only* a page number—no extra text needed.

---

### Editing and Formatting Headers and Footers

Once you’ve added a header or footer, you can edit it just like any other text. You can change the font, size, color, alignment, and spacing—just like in *Formatting Characters and Paragraphs*.

#### How to Edit a Header or Footer

1. Double-click the top or bottom margin of any page where the header/footer appears.
   - Or, go to **Insert > Header** or **Footer**, then choose **Edit Header** or **Edit Footer**.
2. Make your changes:
   - Add or delete text
   - Change the font using the **Home tab**
   - Align text using the alignment buttons in the **Paragraph group**
3. Press **Esc** when done.

> 🔄 **Tip**: Any changes you make to the header or footer on one page will appear on *all* pages that use the same header/footer style.

---

### Creating Different Headers for the First Page

Sometimes, you don’t want the same header (or footer) on the very first page. For example:

- A cover page with no header
- A title page with a different style
- A table of contents with its own header

Word makes this easy with the **Different First Page** option.

#### Step-by-Step: Different First Page Header

1. Double-click the top margin to open the header area.
2. Go to the **Header & Footer tab** (this appears only when you’re editing a header or footer).
3. In the **Options group**, check the box that says **Different First Page**.
4. Now, the first page has a separate header area. Type your title page header here (or leave it blank).
5. Press the **Tab** key to move to the second page’s header area.
6. Type your regular header (e.g., document title).
7. Press **Esc** to save.

> ✅ **Result**: Page 1 has one header (or none), and pages 2+ share another header.

This feature is perfect for formal documents like resumes, cover letters, or reports that start with a title page.

---

### Inserting Date and Time Stamps

Headers and footers are great places for dates. Instead of typing today’s date manually (which becomes outdated), you can insert an **automatic date stamp** that updates every time you open the document.

#### Step-by-Step: Insert Today’s Date in a Header/Footer

1. Open the header or footer area (double-click the top or bottom margin).
2. Place your cursor where you want the date.
3. Go to the **Insert tab** (even though you’re in the header/footer, the Ribbon is still available).
4. In the **Text group**, click **Date & Time**.
5. Choose a format from the list (e.g., *March 15, 2025* or *15-Mar-25*).
6. Optionally, check **Update automatically** so the date refreshes when you reopen the file.
7. Click **OK**.
8. Press **Esc**.

Now, every time you open the document, the date will show today’s date—unless you’ve disabled auto-update.

> 🛠 **Use Case**: In a meeting agenda header, you might want the date to always reflect when the meeting is scheduled.

---

### Customizing Headers and Footers with Graphics

You’re not limited to text in headers and footers. You can add **logos, shapes, borders, or even small icons** to make your document more visually appealing—especially useful for business documents.

#### How to Add a Logo to a Header

1. Open the header area.
2. Go to the **Insert tab**.
3. In the **Illustrations group**, click **Pictures**.
4. Choose **This Device** to insert an image from your computer.
5. Select your logo file (e.g., a .png or .jpg).
6. Resize the logo by dragging its corners.
7. Move it to the left or right side of the header.
8. Press **Esc**.

Your logo now appears in the header of every page.

> 📏 **Tip**: Keep logos small (about 1 inch wide) so they don’t overwhelm the page.

---

### Practical Example: Creating a School Report

Let’s walk through a realistic scenario: You’re writing a 5-page science report.

**Goal**: A clean, professional report with:
- A header showing the report title
- A footer with page numbers
- No header on the first page (title page)

#### Steps:

1. **Create the title page**:
   - Type your report title, your name, and the date.
   - Press **Enter** several times to move to the second page.

2. **Add a header to pages 2–5**:
   - Double-click the top margin of page 2.
   - Go to **Insert > Header > Blank**.
   - Type: *"Biodiversity in Urban Parks – Research Report"*
   - Press **Esc**.

3. **Add page numbers to the footer**:
   - Double-click the bottom margin of page 2.
   - Go to **Insert > Page Number > Bottom of Page > Plain Number**.
   - Press **Esc**.

4. **Remove the header from page 1**:
   - Double-click the top margin of page 1.
   - Go to **Header & Footer tab > Options > check Different First Page**.
   - Delete any text in the first page header.
   - Press **Esc**.

Now your report looks polished:
- Page 1: Clean title page
- Pages 2–5: Title in header, page number in footer

---

### Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even beginners can run into small issues. Here’s what to watch for:

- **Header/footer text appears only on one page**: This happens if you didn’t type in the header/footer area correctly. Double-click the top or bottom margin to re-enter editing mode.

- **Page numbers start at 2 instead of 1**: This usually means the first page is using a different header/footer (e.g., Different First Page is checked). Fix it in **Header & Footer tab > Page Number > Format Page Numbers**.

- **Changes don’t appear on all pages**: Ensure you’re editing the correct header/footer. If you used **Different First Page**, the first page is separate.

- **Text overlaps margins**: Adjust margins in **Layout tab > Margins** if headers/footers are too close to the edge.

---

### Summary of Key Commands

Here’s a quick reference for the commands you’ve learned:

| Task | Where to Find It |
|------|------------------|
| Insert Header | Insert tab > Header |
| Insert Footer | Insert tab > Footer |
| Insert Page Number | Insert tab > Page Number |
| Edit Header/Footer | Double-click top/bottom margin |
| Different First Page | Header & Footer tab > Options > Different First Page |
| Insert Date/Time | Insert tab > Date & Time (in header/footer) |
| Insert Picture | Insert tab > Pictures (in header/footer) |

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Headers and footers** are repeating blocks of text or graphics at the top or bottom of every page in a Word document.
- Use the **Insert tab** to access headers, footers, and page numbers.
- **Automatic page numbering** updates itself when you add or delete pages—never type page numbers manually.
- The **Different First Page** option lets you create a unique header or footer on page 1 (great for title pages).
- You can insert **automatic date stamps** that update when you open the document.
- Headers and footers can include **text, page numbers, dates, logos, and more**—keep them clean and professional.
- Always **double-click the margin** to edit headers or footers, and press **Esc** to return to your main document.

By mastering headers, footers, and page numbers, you’re taking a big step toward creating documents that look intentional, professional, and easy to navigate. Whether it’s a school assignment, a business report, or a personal project, these tools will help you present your work with confidence.

modules.title: Proofing and Reviewing
modules.content:
## Why Proofing Matters: Catching Errors Before They Catch You

Imagine sending a job application with a typo in your name or a critical detail like “5 years of expeirence.” Or submitting a school report where “their” is used instead of “there.” Small slips can make a big impression—usually the wrong one. Microsoft Word’s **proofing tools** exist to help you catch those slips before anyone else does. This chapter shows how to use them, turning what feels like a chore into a quick, confidence-building step.

---

## Running the Spelling and Grammar Check

Every word processor worth its salt includes a **spelling and grammar check**, and Word is no exception. This isn’t about replacing your judgment—it’s about flagging potential issues you might have missed.

### Where to Start
Look at the top of your screen. You’ll see the **Ribbon** with tabs like **Home**, **Insert**, and **Review**. The **Review** tab is your command center for proofing.

1. **Open the Review Tab**
   - Click **Review** in the Ribbon.
   - In the **Proofing** group, you’ll see commands like **Spelling & Grammar** and **Word Count**.

2. **Run a Check**
   - Press **F7** on your keyboard, or click **Spelling & Grammar** in the **Review** tab.
   - Word starts scanning your document from the top, highlighting potential issues one by one.

### How Word Flags Errors
- **Red wavy underline**: Suspected spelling mistake.
- **Blue wavy underline**: Possible grammar issue or word usage problem.
- **Ignore once**: Skip this suggestion but keep checking the rest.
- **Ignore All**: Skip this suggestion for the whole document (use sparingly).
- **Add to Dictionary**: Teach Word to recognize a word it doesn’t know, like a name or technical term.
- **Change**: Accept Word’s suggestion.
- **Change All**: Apply the same correction throughout the document.

> Tip: Word doesn’t know context. It might flag “their” in “Their going to the park” because it expects “they’re.” Always review suggestions—don’t accept them blindly.

### Automatically Check as You Type
You can also have Word check spelling and grammar **in real time**:
- Go to **File > Options > Proofing**.
- Under **When correcting spelling and grammar in Word**, check:
  - **Check spelling as you type**
  - **Check grammar as you type**
  - **Mark grammar errors as you type**

Now, Word underlines errors as you work—no need to press F7 every time. To fix an error, right-click the underlined word or phrase and choose a suggestion.

---

## Using the Thesaurus to Find Synonyms

Sometimes the word you want is on the tip of your tongue—or worse, it’s repeated too often in your document. The **Thesaurus** helps you find alternatives without leaving Word.

### How to Use It
1. Select the word you want to replace.
2. Right-click and choose **Synonyms**.
3. A small menu appears with alternatives like “happy” → “joyful,” “content,” “pleased.”
4. Click a synonym to replace it instantly.

Or, for a full list:
1. With the word selected, go to the **Review** tab.
2. Click **Thesaurus** in the **Proofing** group.
3. A **Thesaurus** pane opens on the right, showing synonyms, part of speech, and related words.
4. Hover over a word and click **Insert** to replace the original.

> Example: “The report was very good.” → “The report was excellent.”
> Or: “The report was outstanding.” to vary your language.

---

## Performing a Find and Replace Operation

What if you realize you’ve misspelled a client’s name throughout a 20-page document? Or you want to update all instances of “Q3” to “third quarter”? Manual editing would take forever. **Find and Replace** does it in seconds.

### Basic Find and Replace
1. Press **Ctrl + H** (Windows) or **Command + H** (Mac).
2. In the **Find what** box, type the text you want to locate (e.g., “expeirence”).
3. In the **Replace with** box, type the correct version (e.g., “experience”).
4. Click **Replace** to change one instance, or **Replace All** to update everything at once.

> Caution: **Replace All** can change things you didn’t intend. Always review changes or use **Find Next** first to confirm each one.

### Advanced Options
Click **More >>** to reveal:
- **Match case**: Only replace words with the same capitalization (e.g., “Word” vs. “word”).
- **Find whole words only**: Avoid replacing parts of other words (e.g., don’t change “cat” in “category”).
- **Use wildcards**: Search for patterns like numbers or dates.
